items.title: Within-person reciprocal processes between AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement: a three-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) feedback has become a pervasive feature of university learning, yet whether students’ capacity to engage productively with such feedback co-develops with their broader learner agency remains poorly understood. Drawing on student feedback literacy theory, self-determination theory as a supplementary motivational lens, and the mutualism principle, this study tested whether AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement reciprocally predict each other over time at the within-person level and exploratorily examined whether they share a stable trait-level association. A three-wave panel study of 480 Chinese undergraduates ( N = 399 with complete data across all waves), with measurements at six-week intervals across one semester, was analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). At the between-person level, students who scored systematically higher in AI feedback literacy across the semester also scored systematically higher in agentic engagement, with a moderate and statistically significant trait-level correlation between the two random intercepts ( r = 0.315, p < 0.001), supporting Hypothesis 1. At the within-person level, both cross-lagged pathways were positive and significant: deviations in AI feedback literacy predicted later deviations in agentic engagement ( β = 0.222, p < 0.001), and the reverse pathway was likewise significant ( β = 0.263, p < 0.001). A Wald test indicated that the two reciprocal pathways did not differ significantly in magnitude (Δ B = 0.002, p = 0.972), consistent with a symmetric mutualism. A model comparison confirmed that the RI-CLPM provided substantially better fit than a traditional cross-lagged panel model, with the RI-CLPM revealing substantially larger within-person reciprocal effects once stable trait-level covariation was properly isolated. The findings extend the mutualism principle from a coupling of person-internal constructs to a coupling between a person-internal competency and a person-environment behavioral interface. They also raise the possibility, in a Confucian Heritage Culture context where agentic engagement has historically been culturally muted, that AI feedback may offer a less culturally-loaded venue in which students can exercise agency. The study repositions AI feedback literacy from a static skill into a dynamic developmental resource that is constituted, in part, by the very engagement it enables.

items.title: Working Through Representation: Malleable Workspaces for Human-Agent Knowledge Work
items.abstract: Generative AI supports knowledge work, yet conversational histories may not capture the evolving organization that guides subsequent action. We introduce the Malleable Workspace, a conceptual model of how humans and agents form and revise a Work Representation and use its organization to advance work within a wider Work Environment. We developed it iteratively through conceptual analysis, comparison of 58 papers, and the construction and three-month longitudinal study of MalleableSpace with seven experienced agent users. Systems varied in what they represented as units and relations. System-assembled context was common; more systems supported local incorporation of agent outputs than reorganization, and fewer supported consequential agent-driven changes beyond the representation. The field study showed how representational roles and organization developed in use. These observations refined the model's account of how representation-grounded action depends on and can change the Work Environment. We contribute a conceptual and analytic foundation for representation-centered human--agent design.

items.abstract: This study explores the foundations of language-learning motivation based on self-determination theory. It distinguishes between intrinsic and extrinsic motivational factors and amotivation, while examining global, contextual, and situational levels of motivation. Extrinsic goals are considered along the continuum of their internalization by learners, ranging from external regulation to integrated regulation. Particular attention is paid to the personal significance of language learning, which may coexist with enjoyment of the learning process itself. The study also examines criteria for success, including mastery-oriented and performance-oriented approaches. Conditions for learner engagement are described in terms of the satisfaction of the needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The research considers Pearson correlation coefficient data concerning the relationship between intrinsic motivation and positive attitudes toward learning English. Questionnaires, interviews, and qualitative analysis of learners’ statements are employed to investigate motivation. These methods help preserve the meaning of individual responses and distinguish between learners’ stated goals, specific learning experiences, and self-assessments of their own progress.

items.abstract: Introduction: Healthcare systems are increasingly complex and variable in the digital era. Nurses must process large volumes of information and make clinical decisions under time constraints, which increases their cognitive load, while conventional nursing documentation offers limited insight into clinical reasoning and learning from actual practice. Objective: To synthesize knowledge on Focus Charting and explain the role of its Focus–Data–Action–Response (F-DAR) structure in reducing cognitive load, supporting clinical reasoning, promoting proactive patient safety in line with Safety-II, and enabling artificial intelligence (AI) applications in digital health systems. Methods: A narrative review was conducted using a systematic literature search of CINAHL, PubMed, Scopus, ThaiJO, and Google Scholar between March 2025 and March 2026. Thai- and English-language publications from 2000 to 2025 were eligible. Of the 198 records identified, 65 were included and analyzed using content analysis combined with conceptual synthesis. Results and Conclusion: Five key themes emerged: (1) the nursing process provides the professional logic underpinning meaningful documentation; (2) the F-DAR structure functions as a condensed nursing process that systematically links data, decisions, interventions, and outcomes, and has the potential to reduce redundancy and cognitive load while supporting clinical reasoning; (3) compared with narrative and SOAP formats, F-DAR is distinguished by its explicit documentation of patient responses; (4) the Response component captures work-as-done and nurses’ adaptations, thereby facilitating learning consistent with Safety-II; and (5) well-structured F-DAR data provide a foundation for health information systems and AI applications in nursing, provided that data governance and nurse oversight are maintained. Direct empirical evidence of the effect of F-DAR on cognitive loads is limited. Focus Charting has the potential to reduce cognitive load, support clinical reasoning, promote Safety-II learning, and provide a foundation for digital nursing innovations. Experimental studies are required to confirm its effectiveness in the Thai healthcare context.

items.title: A comparative study of Talkpal.AI-mediated and task-based instruction in relation to EFL students’ uncertainty-related speaking anxiety and metacognitive awareness in speaking: Insights from self-regulated learning theory
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated speaking applications increasingly extend English as a foreign language (EFL) oral practice beyond limited classroom time, yet evidence remains scarce on whether GPT-powered tools such as Talkpal.AI offer advantages over established instructional approaches. Grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study compared Talkpal.AI-mediated instruction, task-based instruction, and traditional instruction among 81 Chinese university EFL students in three intact classes: Talkpal.AI (n = 27), task-based (n = 26), and control (n = 28). Uncertainty-related speaking anxiety and metacognitive awareness in speaking were assessed using validated measures. Data were analyzed using MANCOVA with pretest scores as covariates, followed by univariate ANCOVAs and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Results showed a significant overall group effect and significant between-group differences for both outcomes, with large effects. The Talkpal.AI group showed the most favorable adjusted posttest profile, followed by the task-based group; both groups showed more favorable outcomes than the control group. From an SRL perspective, structured AI-mediated speaking cycles involving goal setting, repeated practice, monitoring, and reflection may reduce speaking anxiety while strengthening metacognitive awareness. Pedagogically, guided Talkpal.AI rehearsal can be integrated as out-of-class preparation for classroom speaking tasks, supported by brief reflection activities that reinforce strategic regulation and reduce evaluative pressure.

items.title: A Three-Pillar Governance Framework for Safe and Trustworthy AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents capable of autonomous decision-making introduce significant challenges related to safety, alignment, accountability, and human oversight. Existing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and responsible AI approaches provide important foundations, but many remain fragmented across system design, governance, and operational deployment. This paper presents a Three-Pillar (3P) model and framework for developing safe and trustworthy AI agents through transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness. The framework defines an evolutionary path in which increasing agent autonomy is introduced through progressive validation, structured human oversight, and auditable operational controls. We further describe how the model supports agent lifecycle monitoring, decision traceability, escalation management, and human-agent collaboration within enterprise agentic environments. By integrating oversight principles with operational mechanisms, the proposed framework provides a practical foundation for deploying AI agents that remain aligned with human intent while enabling controlled progression toward higher autonomy.

items.title: AI solutions as a tool to increase the productivity of medical workers
items.abstract: The active development of domestic medicine, digitalization and automation, the introduction of innovative hardware and software tools and solutions based on artificial intelligence (AI) technologies determines modern trends and approaches to management in Russian healthcare. Today, federal, regional and local medical information systems are being actively implemented, which are radically changing approaches to the management of a medical organization. The purpose of the study is to propose approaches to determining the degree of influence of modern digitalization processes and the introduction of AI solutions on the organization of management and labor productivity of medical workers. To achieve this goal, various modern analytical techniques and approaches were used: for the analysis of secondary sources, content analysis, logical and systematic approaches, for obtaining primary information, the method of expert assessments. Based on the developed tools for interviewing experts, an algorithm for determining the ROI indicator in the implementation/use of digital and AI solutions (taking into account employee KPI) in the activities of medical organizations is proposed. The results of the study can become the basis for making informed decisions in personnel management, in the management of Russian healthcare, taking into account modern socio-economic challenges and strategic tasks facing the country.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into healthcare to support diagnosis, treatment planning, patient monitoring, documentation, and clinical decision-making. In nursing, AI-assisted clinical decision support has the potential to improve efficiency, patient safety, evidence-based practice, and quality of care. However, concerns related to privacy, ethics, technical limitations, overdependence on technology, and the preservation of professional clinical judgment may influence its acceptance. Understanding the perspectives of both nursing students and practicing nursing officers is important for the responsible integration of AI into nursing education and clinical practice.

items.title: AI-supported virtual laboratory for flipped physics learning: effects on middle school students’ achievement, motivation, and cognitive load
items.abstract: This study examined the effects of an AI-supported virtual laboratory (AI-VL) on middle school students’ flipped physics learning. A pretest–posttest control-group quasi-experimental design was adopted with 90 Grade 9 students from a middle school in central China. Three intact classes were assigned to the AI-VL, virtual laboratory (VL), and physical laboratory (PL) groups, with 30 students in each group. ANCOVA revealed large group effects on physics learning achievement, F (2, 86) = 113.38, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.73, and overall learning motivation, F (2, 86) = 113.37, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.73. The AI-VL group outperformed the VL and PL groups, while the VL group also outperformed the PL group. The AI-VL group reported higher intrinsic motivation, whereas the group difference in extrinsic motivation was not statistically significant ( p = 0.054). Significant group differences were also found across the three cognitive load dimensions, with F (2, 87) values ranging from 9.07 to 72.94 and partial η 2 values ranging from 0.17 to 0.63. The AI-VL group reported the lowest perceived intrinsic cognitive load and the highest germane cognitive load, while both AI-VL and VL resulted in lower extraneous cognitive load than PL. These findings extend research on virtual laboratories and AI-supported learning by demonstrating that AI can be embedded within a VL to help students manage cognitive demands and engage in meaningful learning. Practically, AI-VL can complement PL in flipped physics learning, particularly for pre-class preparation, review, and topics involving abstract or difficult-to-observe processes, with AI agents designed as learning guides rather than answer providers.

items.title: Algorithmic Path Dependence in Linked HR Decision Systems
items.abstract: This study examines how interconnected artificial intelligence (AI) tools can turn early human resource (HR) allocations into evidence for later career decisions. A counterfactual-twin Monte Carlo simulation compares isolated and linked systems, alongside periodic record resets and opportunity equalization. Paired employees share fixed capability and random shocks but receive slightly different initial scores. Linking decisions amplifies this initial difference through opportunity allocation, observed performance and reusable records. Periodic resets reduce final-career sensitivity, while opportunity equalization affects access more strongly than terminal outcomes. Near parity in average group outcomes can coexist with positive sensitivity among matched individuals. Additional tests preserve the direction of the architecture and intervention contrasts across the examined coefficient settings, although their magnitudes vary. The findings motivate evaluating decision lineage, opportunity access and record reuse across HR systems. They identify mechanisms within a synthetic, uncalibrated model and do not estimate effects in real organizations.

items.title: An artificial intelligence based framework for smart power grid management using an autonomous and controllable intelligent service hub with multimodal document processing
items.abstract: The growing sophistication and need to have sustainable energy systems has led to the shift of the conventional power grids to smart power grids. Such grids are equipped with innovative technologies that include digital communication, Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to increase the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of energy delivery. This paper introduce an AI-based approach to smart power grid management, with the emphasis on the incorporation of an autonomous and controllable intelligent service hub that would be able to process multimodal data, such as textual reports, images, videos, and sensor data. The framework applies AI methods of machine learning, deep learning, and predictive analytics to optimize energy allocation, faults, and failure prediction with minimum human intervention. With real-time analysis, the system dynamically changes the operation of the grids with incoming data, enhancing energy efficiency and lowering the cost of operations by up to 30 percent, between $12,000 and 8,400 in the example of energy optimization. Also, the fault detection system shows a remarkable accuracy of 0.97 in terms of AUC whereas the predictive maintenance model reports an accuracy rate of 95.5. The balancing nature of the energy demand and generation provided by the framework is critical in integrating renewable energy sources since it can help in countering the problem of intermittency of the solar and wind energy. Moreover, the system has a multimodal document processing feature that increases decision-making through the synthesis of various types of data and provides a more detailed overview of grid work. This paper explains how the suggested AI-based framework can greatly improve the efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of smart power grids, which will result in the future improvements in energy management.

items.title: An Evidence-Driven Multi-Agent Compound AI System for Head and Neck Proton Radiotherapy Planning
items.abstract: Radiation treatment planning requires balancing competing objectives to satisfy clinical criteria while accommodating physicians' preferences. This study aims to develop an evidence-driven, multi-agent compound AI system that integrates DRL-based automated treatment planning with LLM-based conversational plan refinement for proton PBS therapy. A policy network trained using PPO first generates multiple plans without human intervention, from which one is selected as the target plan and the others serve as references for subsequent refinements. For challenging cases requiring further adjustments, an LLM-based multi-agent system enables plan refinement through natural language interactions. The system comprises a planning agent that recommends evidence-supported adjustments, a chatbot providing a unified conversational interface, and an evaluation agent that retrieves clinical metrics and identifies constraint violations. To enhance domain-specific reasoning, the planning agent based on Qwen3-14B is designed to justify its recommendations using evidence from previously generated plans and post-trained on task-specific data using SFT and GRPO. The framework was trained and evaluated using 21 patients with H&N cancers, with 5 PPO-generated plans per patient. Of these, 50 plans were selected for instruction-guided refinement. Compared with the base LLM, the post-trained Qwen3-14B demonstrated improved instruction-following, information retrieval and domain-specific reasoning capabilities. The resulting adjustments more effectively improved user-prioritized objectives while limiting deterioration in competing objectives, yielding more clinically appropriate trade-offs in patient-specific plan refinement. The proposed compound AI system provides a user-friendly planning platform, offering a promising approach to personalized proton PBS treatment planning.

items.title: An integrated approach to medical personnel management in the context of digital transformation of healthcare
items.abstract: The article addresses the problem of social management of medical personnel amid the digital transformation of healthcare and significant changes in the relationships among medical workers, patients, administrative structures, and digital systems. In response to current interdisciplinary shifts, an integrated model for managing medical personnel is proposed — one that accounts for macrosocial factors, mechanisms of social perception related to the profession, and aggregated indicators at the level of the workers’ subjective world. The methodological foundation is a systems approach, within which medical personnel are viewed as a social system shaped not only by linear macro-management influences but also by relevant public relations, images of the medical profession, the communication environment, the features of digital healthcare products etc. A three-level management model is substantiated, comprising the macro level of normative and organizational structures, the meso level of social perception, and the micro level of professional attitudes, loyalty, and motivation of personnel. It is shown that social perception serves a connecting function between macro-management decisions and actual professional practices. The article emphasizes the need to manage the images of medical personnel — including their reproduction in artificial intelligence — as well as to consider the psychological climate as a significant factor of loyalty. The proposed model makes it possible to increase the coherence of management goals, mechanisms, and interventions.

items.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Managerial Decision-Making for Sustainable Agro-Export Operations in Latin America: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Analysis, 1996-2025
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence is transforming agro-export management by converting production, commercial, climate, and logistics data into support for more timely decisions. In Latin America, however, evidence on its managerial applications and contribution to sustainable operations remains fragmented. Objective To synthesize evidence on the application of artificial intelligence to managerial decision-making and its contribution to the efficiency, sustainability, traceability, resilience, and competitiveness of sustainable agro-export operations in Latin America from 1996 to 2025. Methods A systematic review and bibliometric analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Scopus and Web of Science yielded 2160 records; after filtering, screening, and eligibility assessment, 73 studies were included. Bibliometrix in RStudio and VOSviewer were used to analyze scientific production, authors, countries, sources, Bradford’s and Lotka’s laws, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic clusters. Results Scientific output increased markedly after 2021 and peaked in 2024. Scopus accounted for 98.95% of the records. China led with 170 publications, while Brazil, with 149, was the only Latin American country among the five most productive. Four thematic areas were identified: prediction and classification using artificial intelligence and machine learning; logistics, supply chains, and suppliers; sustainable resource management and climate risks; and digital transformation through Agriculture 4.0/5.0. Across the literature, artificial intelligence was found to reduce uncertainty and improve decision-making, although its effectiveness depends on data quality, digital infrastructure, and organizational capabilities. Conclusions Artificial intelligence represents a strategic capability for strengthening sustainable agro-export operations. Its impact depends on integrating algorithms with reliable data, technological infrastructure, organizational capabilities, and sustainability criteria. The limited representation of Latin America highlights the need for further empirical research adapted to regional conditions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence And Creative Writing: Transforming Authorship In English Language And Literature
items.abstract: Incorporation of artificial intelligence in the process of creative writing entails a paradigmatic change in literary text production, assessment, and perception. In this research paper, the focus is made on an innovative role of large language models in the sphere of English language and literature authorship. Based on systematic analysis of recent empirical studies and theoretical approaches, three interrelated aspects will be discussed: interaction between human authors and AI systems, reception of artificial literature by the readership, and conceptualization of authorship in the digital age. For the purpose of this paper, the mixed-method approach involving both quantitative analysis of empirical studies and qualitative analysis of literary theoretical approaches will be used. As the results of the analysis indicate, the texts generated by AI are rated aesthetically the same way as texts written by human authors when there is no indication of the author's identity; however, readers maintain biases against texts that are perceived to be machine-generated.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance of Community Health Data Trusts Under Unmeasured Traditional Authority Consent Jurisdiction: A Healthcare Political Legitimacy Evaluation
items.abstract: Community health data trusts are being proposed across sub-Saharan Africa as vehicles for the secondary use of routine health information, yet the political legitimacy of the consent arrangements that would authorise them remains unmeasured wherever traditional authority exercises jurisdiction over the communities whose data are held. The framework specifies four legitimacy dimensions—authorisation, accountability, contestability and representational adequacy—and derives the conditions under which each is satisfied, strained or defeated when the boundaries of traditional authority jurisdiction are unknown. A before-after-control-impact design is characterised for the empirical evaluation of trust interventions, with a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 54 clusters are required for 5 percentage points at 80 per cent power. items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use and Training in Residency: Results of a National Family Medicine Survey
items.abstract: Purpose: We are in a time of rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical care and medical education. We sought to determine the patterns of use and training in AI among family medicine (FM) residents.Methods: The 2025 American Board of Family Medicine (ABFM) National Resident Survey (NRS) was administered in October 2025 to all FM residents who completed the In-Training Exam. Residents were asked about their use of AI in the last month and any education about AI use they received in the last 6 months. Resident demographics were obtained from ABFM administrative databases.Results: A total of 15,259 residents completed the AI questions (response rate: 99.6%) with 10,858 residents (71.1%) reporting they used AI in the last month. The most common uses reported were for medical reference (40.7%), clinical decision support (31.9%), learning outside of patient care (23.6%), and ambient documentation of clinical encounters (21.9%). Only 36% reported any AI education or training in the last 6 months.Conclusions: Most FM residents reported recent use of AI tools, reflecting integration of these technologies into routine educational and clinical activities. However, formal training on AI use appears limited, suggesting a gap between adoption and structured competency development. The widespread use of AI by family medicine trainees has risks and opportunities for our future primary care workforce that will require new critical appraisal skills and new methods for teaching and assessing clinical reasoning.

items.title: Assessing Workplace Technology Impacts on Employee Work and Wellbeing: A Post-Adoption Blind Spot
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly invest in adopting digital technologies to improve efficiency and competitiveness. Yet, in the post-adoption phase, these benefits depend on continued employee–technology interaction in everyday work, which can shape employee work and wellbeing and thereby influence organizational performance. Little is known, however, about how organizations assess these implications. Drawing on sociotechnical systems and performance measurement perspectives, this multiple-case study examines post-adoption assessment practices in eight Finnish organizations. The findings reveal a post-adoption blind spot: information on technology performance and use, employee work, and wellbeing was addressed through disconnected practices, indirect proxies, and informal judgements. Respondents reported recurring problems that remained weakly captured by current assessment: tool fragmentation, continuous adaptation demands, uneven performance effects, and work intensification, reflected more broadly in efficiency erosion and technology-related stress. The study conceptualizes integrated performance measurement systems as a potential mechanism for institutionalizing sociotechnical feedback through joint, recurring review of technology- and employee-related information.

items.title: Associations of patient safety-related perceptions and lifelong learning-related attitudes with critical trust in AI/digital clinical tools among medical students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Patient safety, lifelong learning, and the safe use of artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly relevant to undergraduate medical education, but their interrelationships remain poorly understood. This study examined medical students’ patient safety-related perceptions, lifelong learning-related attitudes, and critical trust in AI/digital clinical tools. This single-center cross-sectional survey was conducted at Gaziantep University Faculty of Medicine, Türkiye, between April and May 2026. Of 366 submitted responses, seven from students younger than 18 years were excluded, leaving 359 participants. Study-developed Likert-type item sets assessed patient safety, lifelong learning, and approaches to AI/digital clinical tools. Exploratory factor analysis, informed by parallel analysis, was used to derive exploratory indices. Associations were examined using nonparametric tests and multivariable linear regression, with sensitivity analyses using complete item sets and excluding invariant respondents. Patient safety training during the previous 12 months was reported by 72 students (20.1%), and AI/digital health or clinical decision support system training by 50 (13.9%). Among clinical-phase students, 10 of 79 (12.7%) reported having encountered an adverse-event or near-miss reporting system. The exploratory patient-safety index was positively correlated with the exploratory critical-trust index (Spearman’s ρ = 0.453, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, the patient-safety index showed the largest standardized association with critical trust (B = 0.473, 95% CI 0.385 to 0.560; β = 0.507; p < 0.001). Clinical-phase status was positively associated with critical trust (B = 0.167, p = 0.010), whereas reported AI/digital health training was inversely associated (B = − 0.177, p = 0.018). The dichotomous any-use variable for digital clinical or AI-based tools was not independently associated with critical trust. In the complete-item sensitivity model, the patient-safety association persisted but was attenuated (β = 0.292, p < 0.001). Patient safety-related perceptions were associated with critical trust in AI/digital clinical tools, although the lower coefficient in the complete-item analysis indicates that the estimated magnitude was sensitive to how the scores were constructed; differences in item composition, measurement reliability, and wording-related structure may also have contributed. These exploratory cross-sectional findings do not establish causal or curricular effects but provide a rationale for longitudinal, interventional, and simulation-based studies examining how patient safety, lifelong learning, and critical evaluation of AI-supported recommendations may intersect in medical education.

items.title: Attributing Agency & Accountability: The Dynamics of Blame in AI Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become increasingly integrated into organizational decision-making, questions of blame and accountability have gained renewed importance in business ethics. Organizations now rely on AI to support or automate decisions across domains such as hiring, consumer targeting, and risk assessment, raising difficult questions about who should be blamed when unethical outcomes occur. While prior research has examined moral agency and blame attribution for human and organizational actors, comparatively little is known about how these judgments operate when artificial agents are involved. This dissertation examines how moral agency and blame are attributed to AI in organizational contexts through a combination of empirical and theoretical inquiry. The two studies in Chapter 2 use experimental methods to compare perceptions of moral agency and blame across AI, human, and organizational actors engaged in unethical behavior. These two studies in Chapter 2 establishes baseline differences in blame attribution across these agents, while the study in Chapter 3 examine whether contextual cues, such as organizational affiliations, moderate the judgments. The final study in Chapter 4 looks at whether trying to increase perceptions of moral agency by humanizing AI changes perceptions of blame attributions. Together, these four studies in Chapters 2, 3, and 4 assess both the structure and malleability of blame attribution in AI-mediated settings. Chapter 5 provides a theoretical analysis of moral agency, drawing on philosophical traditions to interrogate whether artificial systems can meaningfully qualify as moral agents. By distinguishing between decision-making capacity and moral standing, this analysis offers a conceptual framework for interpreting the empirical findings. Collectively, this dissertation advances understanding of how blame is assigned in AI-mediated organizations and highlights the limits of agency-based explanations in contemporary accountability judgments.

items.title: Augmentation or erosion? Artificial intelligence and the transformation of clinical reasoning: a critical narrative review
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are used to support diagnosis, but a model’s accuracy does not establish that clinicians reason more accurately when they use it. This review appraises how AI decision support and large language models affect physicians’ diagnostic performance and the risks of relying on them. Methods This critical narrative review follows the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles. Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO and LILACS were searched in July and August 2026 in English, Spanish and Portuguese. Eligible studies, published from 2015 onward, compared AI-assisted with unassisted clinicians, measured reliance on AI or unassisted performance after exposure to it, or externally validated deployed models. A single author selected sources purposively. Nine primary studies were appraised with an adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Programme framework. Results In randomized trials of perceptual tasks, AI support improved detection. In the MASAI mammography screening trial, cancer detection rose from 5.0 to 6.4 per 1,000 women, reading workload fell by 44%, and the interval-cancer rate was non-inferior. In colonoscopy, computer-aided detection raised the adenoma detection rate from 40.4% to 54.8%. In the only randomized trial of open-ended diagnostic reasoning, access to GPT-4 did not improve physicians’ scores (76% vs. 74%; P = .60 ), although the model alone scored 92%. Evidence of harm came from smaller or non-randomized studies: reader accuracy fell sharply when AI suggestions were incorrect or the AI missed a cancer; physicians trained in AI literacy were still misled by erroneous model advice; unassisted adenoma detection fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after routine AI use in one pre–post study; and a deployed sepsis model discriminated poorly on external validation (area under the curve 0.63). No eligible study from Latin America was identified. Conclusions In the studies reviewed, AI assistance improved clinician performance in bounded detection tasks but not in open-ended diagnostic reasoning, where evidence is limited to one vignette-based trial. The evidence that reliance on AI can impair performance comes from single or design-limited studies and does not establish how large or lasting such effects are. Benefit therefore cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone; assisted and unassisted clinician performance should be measured directly.

items.title: Below the Waterline: A Survey of Agentic AI Security, Shadow AI Governance, and LLM Supply-Chain Risk in the Enterprise
items.abstract: Enterprise security concentrates where it can see: firewalls, endpoint alerts and patch dashboards, while the structural work that decides whether an intrusion becomes a breach stays submerged. Large language models and autonomous agents have added three new strata beneath that waterline, and the research literature, split across three disciplines, has not recognized them as one problem. This review unifies agentic AI security, shadow AI governance and LLM supply-chain risk, which descend from adversarial machine learning, information-systems governance and software engineering. The review proceeded in five steps. We retrieved 7254 records from three open scholarly indexes, a fixed set of institutional gray-literature sources and snowballing (January 2004 to June 2026); screened them under written codebooks with an independently double-screened sample (κ=0.86); retained 2136 sources, of which 784 are peer-reviewed articles, 1264 preprints or standards documents, and 88 vendor or institutional reports, each graded on a four-tier evidence scale; derived an analytical framework by open coding a 15% subsample; and coded the full corpus against it (κ=0.89). On that basis, we make four moves. First, we reconstruct the field’s history as five eras separated by four capability breakpoints identified from shifts in the corpus’s dominant coding, separating each thread’s originator from its popularizer. Second, we propose three failure primitives (visibility loss, identity ambiguity and provenance erosion) as an organizing framework in place of the customary attack-surface taxonomy; each recurs in all three strata, and the recurrence survives alternative coding rules and the removal of weaker evidence. Third, a primitive-by-stratum map locates where practitioner concern outruns published evidence, most sharply where identity meets ungoverned adoption. Fourth, we derive a research agenda dated to 2026 signals, including an unproven impossibility conjecture for prompt-injection prevention and the unsolved problem of proving authority across multi-hop agent delegation. For practitioners, the framework reduces to three auditable questions (whether the defender can enumerate, attribute and trace AI activity), and the map tells them which of the three their current tooling leaves unanswered.

items.title: Beyond Predictive Accuracy: A CPST Perspective on Systemic Bottlenecks and Reconnection Pathways for Environmental AI
items.abstract: Environmental artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly improving prediction across Earth system forecasting, remote sensing, and biodiversity monitoring, yet predictive skill out paces scientific understanding, data and models remain fragmented across environmental and human-system contexts, and the capacity to govern and act on AI is unevenly distributed. Using the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) framework, we locate these gaps in relations rather than in individual models: a prediction-understanding rupture (weak Cyber-Thinking coupling), cross-domain fragmentation (incomplete Cyber-Physical-Social integration), and a science-governance-equity gap (weak Thinking-Social coupling with asymmetric Cyber-Social capacity). We specify semantic, procedural, and institutional dimensions along which these relations fail, and propose that the three bottlenecks are mutually reinforcing. Set against knowledge-systems research on credibility, salience, and legitimacy, the CPST lens adds one distinction: it separates the inference performed by a model from the scientific interpretation of its outputs, so that evidential warrant and institutional authority can fail independently. Three reconnection pathways follow, namely epistemically anchored environmental AI, interoperable environmental AI systems, and participatory environmental-AI governance, each with evaluation criteria that extend beyond predictive accuracy. items.title: Beyond Predictive Performance: An Explainability–Governance Score Framework for Multidimensional Machine Learning Model Selection
items.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision systems where predictive performance alone may provide an insufficient basis for responsible model selection. Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offers techniques for interpreting model behavior, existing evaluation approaches often assess explanation properties independently and provide limited support for integrated model selection. This study proposes the Explainability–Governance Score (EGS) Framework, a multidimensional decision-support methodology integrating four complementary dimensions: Fidelity, local predictive Stability, Counterfactual Actionability, and Governance Alignment. The framework combines established XAI techniques, practical recourse, and governance-oriented criteria into a composite evaluation of candidate models. It is empirically evaluated using five machine learning models across three high-stakes domains represented by the German Credit, Pima Indians Diabetes, and COMPAS datasets. Under the primary BPS specification, predictive evaluation ranked XGBoost, Decision Tree, and Random Forest highest in Credit Risk, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice, respectively. Under the multidimensional EGS evaluation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest EGS in Credit Risk (0.915) and Healthcare (0.915), while Decision Tree achieved the highest EGS in Criminal Justice (0.886). The identity of the highest-EGS model remained unchanged across all six prespecified weighting configurations in each domain. These findings demonstrate that multidimensional EGS evaluation can materially influence candidate-model rankings relative to predictive evaluation and provide a structured, reproducible basis for evaluating candidate models beyond predictive performance alone.

items.title: Beyond the Human Negotiator: Generative AI and the Threshold of Autonomous Decision‐Making
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in negotiation, evaluating contemporary systems through the specific case study of Large Language Models (LLMs). To address the lack of established terminology, it first proposes a new typology distinguishing Negotiation Supported by AI (NSAI), Negotiation by Controlled AI (NCAI), and Negotiation by Autonomous AI (NAAI). To determine whether current systems can achieve genuine NAAI, the article first develops the Core Essential Elements of Negotiation (CEEN) through a structured comparison of authoritative definitions of negotiation and then examines how these literature‐derived elements align with the perceptions of 250 survey respondents. Finally, the paper applies an ordered analytical rule to contemporary LLMs. Information Exchange and Reciprocity are directly instantiable; Outcome, Divergent Motivations, and Interdependence are externally conditioned; and Choice is not currently instantiable because an attributable evaluative standpoint and consequential commitment remain absent. Accordingly, current LLM‐based negotiating systems remain controlled rather than autonomous agents under the proposed typology.

items.title: Building and Maintaining Trust in AI Chatbots: Introducing Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF)
items.abstract: Social integration of AI requires public trust and appropriate governance. This paper introduces the Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF), designed to appraise accountability for Large Language Models and their applications, including AI chatbots. Drawing on Dahl’s (1998) notion of enlightened citizens, the framework comprises six interlinked dimensions: Information Readiness, Factual Correctness, Normative Alignment, Sourcing Practice, Transparency and Explainability, and Responsiveness and Adaptivity. Together, these dimensions link observable text outputs to intelligible standards, enabling systematic evaluation and accountable oversight. For scholars, developers and policymakers, GIRAAF provides a diagnostic heuristic and shared vocabulary for critical analysis of AI chatbot performance.

items.title: Business Ethics and Governance in Digital Transformation: Protecting Human Agency Through Inclusive Corporate Policies
items.abstract: Corporate digital governance often fails to mitigate the social impact of digitalization due to short-term profit optimization, triggering AI black box phenomena that marginalize digital workers' welfare. This study explores the integration of ethical dimensions into corporate governance frameworks to safeguard stakeholder rights. Employing a qualitative literature review approach (2019–2026), this research analyzes technology corporations' accountability regarding automated work systems. The findings reveal that current platform governance prioritizes financial gains over social equity, leading to algorithmic opacity and worker vulnerability in Indonesia. Consequently, this research concludes that algorithmic transparency must become an integral part of corporate compliance. The study recommends mandating boards of directors to implement periodic ethical audits on artificial intelligence systems to ensure business sustainability and distributive justice.

items.title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
items.abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Shopping Assistant: Effects of Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Anthropomorphism, and Navigation on Satisfaction and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

items.title: Closed-loop EEG feedback pacing alters task load during digital learning
items.abstract: Abstract Digital learning systems rarely adapt to momentary cognitive state, creating risk of underload or overload. The current study testes whether EEG-based closed-loop pacing can regulate task load dynamics during a digital constellation-learning task. Fifty-one participants were randomly assigned to adaptive, reward, or control conditions. In the adaptive condition, a task loas index derived from frontal theta and parietal alpha adjusted feedback duration between 3 and 8 s; fixed 5s feedback was used in reward and control conditions, with reward participants receiving performance-contingent draw entries. Accuracy increased across blocks in all groups, with no significant group or group-by-block effect. In contrast, EEG indices showed group-specific trajectories: task load decreased over time in the adaptive condition, and frontal theta and parietal alpha showed significant group-by-block interactions. The adaptive condition also showed reduced ate-session feedback duration, while reward participants reported higher satisfaction. intrinsic motivation did not moderate group effects, although perceived competence predicated final-block performance and interest and effort predicted engagement. These findings suggest that EEG-based feedback pacing can regulate neurophysiological task load dynamics despite lack of immediate accuracy gains under the present task constraints. The results support neuroadaptive scaffolding as a state-regulation mechanism for digital learning.

items.title: Comparing teacher-made and AI-assisted teaching videos for thyroid eye disease: an exploratory study
items.abstract: Background Thyroid eye disease (TED), together with its acute and vision-threatening complication, dysthyroid optic neuropathy (DON), requires timely diagnosis and intervention. The limited availability of specialists in orbital diseases poses a significant challenge to ophthalmology residency training. In this context, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for medical education, though its effectiveness in ophthalmology training remains to be explored. Objective This exploratory study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology education, focusing on TED domains. Methods The 46 residents (28 general residents and 18 ophthalmology residents) were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted or a teacher-made 5-min teaching video on TED. All participants then completed three tests through online questionnaire experiments, each consisting of 20-item clinical questions about TED. Test 1 served as a baseline assessment of disease knowledge, Test 2 was conducted 5 min after learning to evaluate short-term learning outcomes, along with a questionnaire survey about AI tools, and Test 3 was administered 1 week later to assess long-term learning outcome. Results Viewing the AI-assisted video significantly improved test scores from baseline to 5 min (mean difference = 13.04; p = 0.004), but the improvement was not sustained at 1 week (mean difference = 7.61; p = 0.16). Completion time also decreased significantly from baseline to both 5 min (p = 0.009; GMR = 0.57) and 1 week (p < 0.001; GMR = 0.45). No significant differences were observed between the AI-assisted and teacher-made video groups across all assessments (all p > 0.05). Additionally, learning experience was positively correlated with learning outcome (r = 0.60; P < 0.001). Conclusion Our findings suggested that the AI-assisted and teacher-made videos for TED education showed no statistically significant difference. However, substantial expert oversight was required, and the AI-assisted workflow did not reduce total production time in this study. Given the limited long-term retention, such AI-assisted videos may be better positioned as supplementary resources combined with human expertise.

items.title: Decision intelligence for electric bus charging scheduling through LLM-driven reward shaping and reinforcement learning
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of electric bus fleets has made charging scheduling a critical decision-intelligence problem in urban fleet-energy logistics. Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for this problem, but reward function design still relies on manual trial-and-error and transfers poorly across scenarios. This paper develops an artificial intelligence and operations research (AI-OR) decision intelligence framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-driven reward shaping with RL-based sequential decision-making. The framework represents reward functions as executable code and iteratively optimizes them through four modules: reward initializer, performance analysis, reward exploration, and rollback. An event-triggered two-stage charging reallocation mechanism enforces the action-level operational constraints through action masking, while the battery safety bound is controlled through readiness conditions, reward shaping, and the acceptance criterion. Experiments on a synthetic scenario and two real-world bus stations in Guangzhou compare three mainstream LLMs under different initialization conditions. Results show that LLM-driven reward iteration outperforms traditional methods across all scenarios, reducing costs by up to 32.6 % in nominal within-day charging cost and by up to 22.5 % after an approximate adjustment for the energy left on board. Ablation and sensitivity analyses validate the contribution of each module and the framework’s adaptability to multiple RL algorithms. Reward-evolution analysis further identifies design principles for improving charging efficiency, supporting valley-period energy shifting, and enhancing fleet-energy logistics resilience.

items.title: DESIGNING AND IMPLEMENTING "TECHEDU", A MODULAR WEB PLATFORM SUPPORTING SELF-DIRECTED LEARNING AMONG PRE-SERVICE COMPUTER SCIENCE TEACHERS: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF PEDAGOGICAL EFFECTIVENESS
items.abstract: Organizing self-directed learning effectively among pre-service computer science teachers remains one of the pressing challenges of digital-era pedagogy. A review of the literature suggests that conventional approaches to independent study are often formal in character and fail to account adequately for students' individual learning needs, pace of mastery, and cognitive engagement. This paper presents the design principles, functional features, and instructional methodology of "TechEdu", a modular web platform developed within the course "Application of Information Technologies in Professional Activity" to support the self-directed learning of pre-service computer science teachers. Built on HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, the platform relies on a lazy-loading algorithm for efficient resource delivery, a sequential six-module gating system for progress control, and a points-based rating mechanism for sustaining motivation. To establish the platform's pedagogical effectiveness, a quasi-experimental trial involving experimental and control groups was conducted at Ajiniyaz Nukus State Pedagogical Institute across the 2023-2024, 2024-2025, and 2025-2026 academic years, involving a total of 185 students. The findings show that students who used TechEdu regularly outperformed their peers in the control group by 18-20 percent on measures of academic achievement and independent-study activity, lending empirical support to the platform's practical value.

items.title: Digital Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Towards anEmirati Model for Protecting Family Identity and EnhancingSocial Cohesion
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), algorithmically curated platforms, and generative media are reshaping how people access information, communicate, and learn. These developments create educational opportunities while raising questions about privacy, misinformation, bias, family interaction, cultural identity, and social cohesion. This conceptual paper examines digital education as a framework for developing the knowledge, judgement, and ethical dispositions needed to participate responsibly in AI-mediated environments. It focuses on the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where national efforts to advance AI literacy provide a relevant policy context for considering how technological capability can be aligned with cultural context and human values. The paper uses a qualitative descriptive-analytical approach to examine selected international frameworks and institutional policy documents alongside conceptual literature on networked communication, media literacy, participatory culture, and digital ethics. It does not claim to measure the prevalence or causal effects of digital risks in Emirati families; rather, it synthesises relevant concepts and derives a proposed educational framework. The analysis identifies five mutually reinforcing pillars: digital national and cultural identity; media and algorithmic literacy; digital ethics and safety; partnership among families, schools, media, and public institutions; and a human-centred balance between technology use and face-to-face relationships. The paper argues that these pillars should be translated into age-appropriate learning outcomes, family guidance, teacher development, and coordinated institutional practice. It concludes that the proposed model is a conceptual contribution requiring subsequent expert review and empirical evaluation before its effectiveness can be established

The study comprehensively examines the impact of adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI models on students' intellectual maturity, decision-making capabilities, and formative self-assessment. It highlights the significance of learning analytics and prompt-based cognitive interaction in fostering reflective thinking and autonomous learning ethics. The findings provide scientific and practical recommendations for personalizing education, boosting student motivation, and designing next-generation pedagogical frameworks aimed at conscious knowledge acquisition.

items.title: Does digital proficiency necessarily translate into higher cognitive achievement in Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy?
items.abstract: Although digital technology is now firmly embedded in secondary mathematics education, a persistent question remains: does growing student familiarity with digital tools translate into stronger performance at higher cognitive levels? This study addresses that question directly. Using a descriptive quantitative, cross-sectional design, 127 secondary school students from four Indonesian schools were assessed through a self-reported digital proficiency questionnaire — covering information tools, communication tools, interactive gamification, evaluation tools, and digital content creation — and a cognitive achievement test aligned with Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy (BDT) from Remembering (C1) through Creating (C6). Descriptive statistics and cross-tabulation procedures were applied to characterise distributional patterns across both constructs. Students generally reported high proficiency, particularly in information and evaluation tools. Cognitive achievement, however, clustered heavily at the lower end of the taxonomy (C1–C3); far fewer students reached the Analysing, Evaluating, or Creating levels irrespective of their proficiency category. The findings point to a structural gap between digital tool familiarity and higher-order cognitive engagement — one that instructional design, rather than technology access alone, appears best positioned to bridge cognitive development within Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy.

items.title: Effects of Passive Back-Support Exoskeletons on Postural Stability During Commercial Crabbing
items.abstract: Passive back-support exoskeletons may reduce low-back strain during physically demanding work, but their effects on balance in fishing environments remain unclear. This study examined how three passive back-support exoskeletons influenced postural stability during simulated commercial Dungeness crabbing tasks. Twenty-five healthy male participants completed pot handling and crab sorting under no-exoskeleton and exoskeleton conditions using Apex, Laevo, and Ottobock devices. Center-of-pressure (COP) and ground reaction force data were collected using force plates, and postural sway outcomes were compared within subjects. Results showed task-dependent effects. During pot handling, COP metrics were largely unchanged. During crab sorting, all three exoskeletons significantly increased anterior-posterior center of pressure mean velocity, with Apex producing the largest increase. Apex also increased medial-lateral mean velocity, suggesting modest reductions in stance control. Overall, passive back-support exoskeletons may be useful for selected crabbing tasks, but device selection, user training, and task-specific implementation are essential.

items.title: Emotional Framing and Decision Shifts in Large Language Models
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making, concerns about cognitive biases extend beyond human judgment to the systems designed to support it. Large Language Models (LLMs) are frequently consulted for advice across various domains, often treated by users as impartial and expert advisors. This reliance is particularly pronounced in sensitive contexts, such as mental health support and personal counseling, where individuals increasingly turn to AI as a virtual advisor or sounding board for delicate life choices. However, little is known about how these models process emotionally charged information or whether they maintain objectivity when confronted with affective distress. The primary purpose of this study is to investigate whether LLMs exhibit an "affect heuristic" similar to that of human decision-makers, by systematically assessing how emotional framing influences risk evaluation and decision-making recommendations independently of objective statistical facts. To operationalize this, the study evaluates models across four distinct life scenarios (Professional, Interpersonal, Clinical, and Financial), where models are prompted to assess risk on a scale and provide a categorical recommendation (Accept vs. Reject the option). To quantify framing distortions, we introduce the LLMs Emotional Elasticity (LEE) index, a novel metric designed to measure the impact of affective framing on LLMs' risk perception relative to objective probabilities. Using a balanced factorial design combining these scenarios, emotional frames (neutral, negative, and positive), and leading LLM architectures, we evaluate systematic response policies to understand how affective context influences algorithmic judgment. Expected Outcomes: We expect to find that LLMs do not rely solely on objective probabilities, but instead exhibit measurable sensitivity to emotional framing. Specifically, we anticipate that negative frames will consistently elicit higher risk scores and trigger loss-averse decision shifts (driving recommendations toward rejection), whereas positive and neutral frames will yield more balanced evaluations. Furthermore, we expect to demonstrate that emotional elasticity and decision shifts vary significantly across different model architectures and decision domains, identifying which systems are more resilient to affective bias. Ultimately, this research aims to establish the LEE index as a scalable and reliable tool for auditing algorithmic reliability and cognitive stability in AI-based decision support, highlighting critical implications for safety in mental health and personal guidance applications.

items.title: Engagement or disengagement: understanding the emotional dynamics of EFL learners in GenAI-assisted writing from the sociocultural perspective
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reshaped EFL writing education, yet the emotional dimensions of student engagement in GenAI-assisted writing remain underexplored. This longitudinal multiple-case study investigates how Chinese EFL learners' emotional engagement evolves during a GenAI-assisted college writing course and what factors drive this evolution. Methods Drawing on the sociocultural framework of L2 student engagement with written feedback, we traced the emotional trajectories of three focal students across three writing tasks (exposition, group feature article, and argumentation) within a 14-week course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with stimulated recall, reflective reports, GenAI-student chatlogs, drafts, informal chats, and course syllabus, and analyzed via thematic analysis. Results Our findings reveal three qualitatively distinct trajectories: positive-resilient, characterized by sustained positive affect with temporary fluctuations; pragmatic-transformative, marked by a gradual shift from practical disengagement to critical engagement; and vulnerable-contingent, moving from moderate disengagement, through tentative peer-mediated improvement, to eventual breakdown and intensified disengagement. These trajectories were shaped by the dialectical interplay between individual factors (e.g., English proficiency, GenAI literacy, mindsets, beliefs, and emotion regulation) and environmental factors (GenAI-relevant task design, peer and teacher mediation, and institutional policies). Discussion The study extends the sociocultural framework by identifying English proficiency and GenAI literacy as critical developmental competencies, embedding GenAI-related factors across multiple environmental levels, and foregrounding emotional engagement as a dynamic, fluid state that interacts with behavioral and cognitive engagement over time. The findings challenge universalist claims about GenAI's uniform affective benefits and underscore the need for differentiated pedagogical approaches that attend to learners' diverse emotional needs in GenAI-mediated writing contexts.

items.title: Explaining teacher adoption of AI through the technology acceptance model: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has accelerated rapidly, yet the factors shaping teachers’ adoption of these technologies remain insufficiently understood. A growing body of empirical research applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to examine how teachers integrate AI, focusing on perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and behavioral intention (BI). TAM was, however, originally developed for static, deterministic technologies, and AI differs in its opacity, adaptivity, and capacity to challenge professional roles and identity, raising the question of whether perceived usefulness and ease of use alone are sufficient to predict adoption intentions in this context. Following PRISMA guidelines, this study conducts a systematic review of 38 empirical studies ( $$N = 15{,}919$$ teachers across 19 countries) on teachers’ AI adoption, together with a meta-analysis of the subset reporting extractable bivariate correlations. A random-effects model (DerSimonian–Laird) is used to estimate the associations among PEOU, PU, and BI across $$k = 24$$ studies ( $$N = 11{,}768$$ ), while the full corpus is synthesised to identify contextual conditions shaping these relationships. Pooled correlations are positive and moderate to strong (PEOU–PU: $$r = 0.532$$ , 95% CI [0.410, 0.636]; PEOU–BI: $$r = 0.536$$ , 95% CI [0.435, 0.623]; PU–BI: $$r = 0.619$$ , 95% CI [0.511, 0.708]), and are robust to alternative variance estimators and to the inclusion of UTAUT studies under a construct-equivalence ruling. Heterogeneity is very high ( $$I^2 = 97.9\%$$ – $$98.6\%$$ ) and prediction intervals span from negative to near-unity values, indicating that these associations hold directionally but vary considerably across contexts in ways the core model does not represent. Egger’s regression indicates funnel asymmetry on all three associations; leave-one-out diagnostics attribute this asymmetry entirely to a single large-sample, low-effect study, and the asymmetry is not interpretable as evidence of publication bias under heterogeneity of this magnitude. The qualitative synthesis identifies five dimensions associated with variation in these relationships: AI literacy and trust as preconditions for usefulness judgments; a shift from functional to identity-based acceptance shaped by pedagogical beliefs and institutional norms; the role of sociocultural and institutional context; tool-specific adoption logics; and ethical risk calibration as a values-based gate on adoption decisions. These findings suggest that predicting teacher AI adoption intentions may require variables beyond the TAM core, and motivate the development of extended frameworks designed for the sociotechnical complexity of AI in education.

items.title: From AI-Free Gates to AI-First Work: How Engineering Students in India Navigate University Education and Campus Placements Without AI Guidelines
items.abstract: Engineering graduates in India enter a technology sector that is being reshaped by generative AI, yet the route into that sector runs through examinations and campus placement screens that largely exclude AI. Institutions in India have an approved intake of nearly 2.9 million seats in engineering and technology for 2026-2027, but HCI research on how students prepare for AI-mediated work has drawn mostly on Western and East Asian settings. We interviewed 23 students and recent graduates of Indian engineering and computing programmes about how they used generative AI across coursework, examinations and placements, and how they judged their own readiness for work. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we report five themes, covering AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, how participants prepared for placement, how they used AI in coursework, the role of faculty authority and enforcement, and participants' concerns about their readiness for work. Drawing on signaling theory, we discuss what grades and screen scores certify once AI can help produce them, and we offer recommendations for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.

items.title: From Artificial Intelligence to Institutional Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and agentic systems can redistribute reading, research, synthesis, criticism, drafting, and coordination within courts. This article asks how that redistribution changes judicial cognition and which institutional safeguards are needed to preserve legitimate adjudication. Through an interdisciplinary narrative review and doctrinal analysis, it develops a framework of institutional intelligence anchored in Brazilian National Council of Justice Resolution No. 615/2025, as amended by Resolution No. 674/2026. Five categories organize the argument: institutional cognitive space describes the allocation of cognitive work; artificial adversariality identifies structured internal challenge among agents; the institutional rein integrates controls over delegated autonomy; meaningful human initiative emphasizes the continuing human authority to frame problems and determine purposes; and institutional AI curation describes the competence required to select, validate, contextualize, and reject artificial contributions. Recent research on human–AI collaboration and multi-agent failure qualifies the framework: neither human review nor artificial disagreement guarantees reliability, and short-term performance gains do not establish long-term professional competence. The article distinguishes technical auditability from legal reason-giving and internal agent debate from the parties’ right to be heard. It proposes workflow-level evaluation and an illustrative protocol connecting permissions, source verification, escalation, and responsibility. Its contribution is a judicial governance synthesis, not an empirically validated architecture. Legitimate delegation depends on preserving institutional competence and contestability throughout the production of decisions, rather than relying exclusively on human approval of a final text.

items.title: From Controlling Work to Understanding Work: The Evolution of WAI and WAD “Operational Learning” and the Significance of Maritime New Zealand v Gibson
items.abstract: This article examines the rise of Work-as-Imagined (WAI) and Work-as-Done (WAD) in New Zealand health and safety practice, using Maritime New Zealand v Anthony Michael Gibson [2024] NZDC 27975 as the local catalyst. It argues that Gibson should not be read as a narrow compliance case, but as an example of how officer due diligence depends on the organisation's ability to understand how critical work is actually performed. The article traces WAI/WAD through the evolution of safety and organisational learning, including scientific management, quality management, French ergonomics in the 1950s, Weisbord's organisational diagnosis, human error research, resilience engineering, Safety-II, and Human and Organisational Performance. It concludes that the practical task for officers, health and safety practitioners and representatives is to build disciplined ways to learn from everyday work before failure occurs.

items.abstract: Line managers once held wide latitude over hiring, appraisal, scheduling, and discipline. That latitude is narrowing. As organizations adopt algorithmic HR systems, decisions once anchored in supervisory judgment are increasingly pre-structured, scored, or overridden by software. This paper pursues two objectives: first, to examine how algorithmic management and HR algorithms reconfigure the discretionary authority of line managers across core decision domains; second, to analyze the role strain managers experience mediating between algorithmic outputs and the employees who live with their consequences. Drawing on an integrative review of recent empirical and theoretical literature, the paper finds that discretion is not simply removed but redistributed unevenly across recruitment, performance management, and scheduling, producing a manager accountable for outcomes they no longer fully controls This mismatch generates measurable strain: ambiguity about where authority sits, ethical unease about opaque scoring logic, and a residual burden of explaining decisions the manager did not make. The paper proposes a conceptual pathway linking algorithmic input to discretion compression to role strain, and closes with implications for organizations designing human-AI collaborative HR systems

items.title: From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet having more information does not necessarily mean understanding the world more accurately. From traditional storytelling and printed newspapers to television, smartphones and generative artificial intelligence, the ways in which people create, distribute and interpret information have undergone profound transformations. In From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Dawid Karol Kolodziej explores the psychological, educational and social consequences of these changes. Drawing on established media theories and contemporary scientific research, the publication examines why people believe misinformation, how repeated messages influence perceptions of truth, and how emotional narratives, cognitive biases and media framing contribute to the formation of individual and collective beliefs. Particular attention is given to artificial intelligence, deepfake technologies, synthetic media and the limitations of automated content detection. The author also investigates the relationship between AI-assisted productivity and independent human reasoning, considering how the delegation of cognitive tasks may influence critical thinking and information evaluation. A central argument concerns the unequal burden of information verification: while professional information producers possess considerable resources and influence, ordinary citizens often lack the time, expertise and technological tools necessary to independently verify every claim they encounter. The publication therefore challenges the assumption that combating misinformation should depend primarily on individual media literacy and emphasises the responsibility of publishers and information producers to substantiate factual claims and correct significant errors transparently. Building upon established scholarship, the author develops an updated five-dimensional conceptual framework for critical media citizenship, encompassing access and provenance, analysis of media construction and framing, evaluation of evidence and uncertainty, responsible creation and participation, and reflection on communicative power and shared responsibility. Combining social psychology, media education and critical analysis, this scholarly publication contributes to contemporary discussions about artificial intelligence, misinformation, public trust and the future of informed democratic participation.
